questions.question: How does the browser render a page — from HTML to pixels?
questions.title: How Browsers Render
questions.direct_answer: Pipeline: parse HTML → DOM tree; parse CSS → CSSOM; combine → render tree (visible nodes only). Then LAYOUT computes geometry (x/y/width/height per visible node), PAINT fills pixels per layer, COMPOSITE combines layers on the GPU. Changes then differ in cost: geometry changes trigger reflow (expensive, cascades), visual-only changes trigger repaint, and transform/opacity changes hit only the compositor — the 60fps properties.

sections.title: Quick Revision
sections.content: Pipeline: parse HTML → DOM tree; parse CSS → CSSOM; combine → render tree (visible nodes only). Then LAYOUT computes geometry (x/y/width/height per visible node), PAINT fills pixels per layer, COMPOSITE combines layers on the GPU. Changes then differ in cost: geometry changes trigger reflow (expensive, cascades), visual-only changes trigger repaint, and transform/opacity changes hit only the compositor — the 60fps properties.

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
The pipeline, verified structure:

```
HTML bytes → tokenizer → DOM tree (the document's structure)
CSS bytes  → CSSOM (the cascade's rule tree)
DOM + CSSOM → RENDER TREE (only VISIBLE nodes: display:none excluded,
               head excluded; visibility:hidden IS in the tree, just unpainted)

RENDER TREE → LAYOUT: compute geometry for every visible node
             (a box's x, y, width, height — reflow = recompute this)
           → PAINT: fill pixels — text, colors, images, shadows, per layer
           → COMPOSITE: GPU stacks layers in the right order
```

The change-cost ladder (what interviewers probe next):
```
transform, opacity  → COMPOSITOR ONLY  — GPU handles it; 60fps animations ✓
color, background   → REPAINT          — repaint the layer, no geometry
width, font-size,
content change      → REFLOW + repaint — recompute geometry for the
                                        node AND everything its change
                                        affects — the expensive tier
```

Layout thrashing (the classic anti-pattern, verified as a mechanism):
```js
// READ (forces sync layout) then WRITE (invalidates) in a LOOP:
for (const el of items) {
  el.style.height = el.offsetHeight + 10 + 'px';  // offsetHeight READ
}   // each iteration: read after a pending write → browser MUST reflow NOW
// FIX: batch — read ALL, then write ALL (or FastDOM does this for you)
```
This is why 'why is my animation janky?' answers are almost always: you're animating a layout property (top/left/width) instead of transform.

sections.title: Mental Model
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart LR
    H[HTML] --> DOM[DOM tree]
    C[CSS] --> CSSOM[CSSOM]
    DOM & CSSOM --> RT[render tree: visible only]
    RT --> L[layout: geometry] --> P[paint: pixels per layer] --> G[composite: GPU layers]
    CH{change type}
    CH -->|transform/opacity| CO[compositor only — 60fps]
    CH -->|color| RP[repaint]
    CH -->|geometry| RF[reflow + repaint — cascade]
```

sections.title: Deep Dive
sections.content:
Why CSS is render-blocking by design (the tradeoff to articulate): the browser can't do layout without knowing final styles — painting with half the CSS then repainting when the rest arrives means double work and visible flashing (FOUC). So HTML parsing continues but first paint WAITS for the CSSOM. The optimization menu: media-split stylesheets (print/mobile — the non-matching ones don't block), preload + inline critical CSS (above-the-fold styles in a style tag, the rest async), and Minify/CDN the critical file. Scripts: sync scripts block the parser AND wait on CSSOM; async runs when downloaded (order unguaranteed — analytics tags); defer runs in order after parsing (app code — the default choice).

The composite layer model (the perf unlock): the browser promotes elements to their own GPU layers (transform: translateZ(0), will-change: transform — the promotion hints) so a moving element doesn't force repainting what's UNDER it — the compositor just repositions layers. Over-promotion costs memory (each layer is a texture) and can cause the opposite problem (too many layers exhaust GPU memory). The modern guidance: animate transform/opacity, let the browser decide promotion, use will-change sparingly and remove it after the animation.

The event-loop tie-in (the completeness close): all this runs on the main thread, which ALSO runs your JS. A long task (any JS > 50ms) blocks layout/paint AND input — the 'page froze' experience. requestAnimationFrame schedules work right before the next paint (the right place for animation reads/writes); requestIdleCallback schedules into idle time (non-urgent background work). The 60fps budget: 16.6ms per frame for ALL of script + layout + paint + composite — the number that turns 'it feels slow' into arithmetic.
